description: A team of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science students.
summary:
Selene is a free web app for choosing where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. There the Sun skims the horizon, so a single ridge can cut solar power for days, and Earth can drop behind the terrain and break direct radio contact. Pick a landing site and an arrival date, and Selene shows, hour by hour, when the Sun is up and when Earth is in view, measured against the real terrain skyline.

It addresses the challenge directly: it ranks 28 sites, including Apollo landings, recent robotic landers and NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions, accepts any custom point, compares sites side by side, shows what a launch delay does, and plays a whole stay in a 3D view from the lander.

It matters because power and communication decide whether a polar mission survives. Every result comes from NASA LRO LOLA terrain and JPL DE440 ephemerides, checked against JPL Horizons, so planners, students and the public can trust what they see.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Selene helps you choose where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. At the pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a single ridge can mean days without solar power, and Earth can sink behind the terrain and cut direct radio contact. Pick a landing site and an arrival date, and Selene shows, hour by hour, when the Sun is up and when Earth is in view, measured against the real terrain skyline, not a flat horizon.

- Ranks 28 sites by how much of a 7, 14 or 30-day stay each one is both sunlit and in contact with Earth: Apollo landings, recent landers (IM-1, IM-2, Blue Ghost 1, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e 4 and 6), south-polar reference points and NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions. You can also click any point on the polar map or type coordinates.

- "Stand at the lander": a 360-degree 3D view built from real terrain, with the Sun and Earth where they really are. Press Play to watch the whole stay; countdowns show the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earth-rise.

- Five plain numbers per site, with separate power and radio grades: time sunlit, longest night (what a battery must cover), time Earth is in view, longest radio silence, and time lit and in contact together.

- Polar Atlas maps: where the Sun and Earth are up right now, how much of your stay each spot is lit, how steep the ground is, and a finder for spots that are both well lit and gently sloped.

- Launch Windows: the Slip Explorer shows what arriving days later does to a site, and Site Shift shows the effect of landing a little off target.

- Compare up to four sites on the same dates (double-click a site to add it), with the best value in each row highlighted. Star favourites to keep them on the home page.

- Also: battery sizing for a given solar array and load, lunar eclipse detection, a 3D Moon lit by the real Sun (including Earth's shadow during eclipses), shareable links, CSV/JSON/text export, Simple and Expert modes, four themes and a guided tour.

HOW IT WORKS

1. A Python pipeline computes Sun and Earth positions from JPL's DE440 ephemeris (via Skyfield), rotated into the Moon-fixed frame with NAIF SPICE kernels, stored hourly for 2025 to 2035.

2. Each site's skyline is traced across NASA's LRO LOLA 80 m south-polar terrain along 720 bearings out to 200 km, including the Moon's curvature.

3. In the browser, the engine samples the stay every 10 minutes and counts the Sun or Earth as up only when it clears that skyline. Heavy work (maps, 3D shading) runs in background threads so the app stays responsive.

Validation: Sun and Earth directions match 42 reference values from JPL Horizons to within 0.00002 degrees; our illumination results match NASA PGDA's published 18.6-year sunlight and Earth-visibility maps at 2,000 random polar points (correlation 0.99, mean difference 0.8 percentage points); 306 automated tests run on every change.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Checking a polar landing site normally means combining ephemeris tools, terrain data and spreadsheets by hand. Selene does it in seconds, in a web browser, with no install or account. Early-stage mission planners get a fast, transparent first look at power and communication risk, including what a launch slip costs, before detailed analysis. Students, teachers and the public can see why the lunar south pole is so hard, and so valuable, to land at. We hope it makes Artemis-era exploration easier to understand and to plan.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

TypeScript, React, Three.js (3D), D3 (charts), Zustand, Vite and Tailwind CSS for the web app; Python with Skyfield, NumPy and Pillow for the data pipeline; Vitest for testing; hosted on Vercel. Data: NASA LRO LOLA, JPL DE440 and Horizons, NAIF SPICE, NASA PGDA, NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit. No special hardware.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- You "stand" at the lander and watch the real Sun and Earth move around the real skyline, rather than reading a table.

- Each site on the home page is drawn as a mission patch whose ring is that site's real skyline, with the Sun and Earth on it.

- The 3D Moon is lit by the actual Sun for your date: long terrain shadows at sunrise and sunset, and Earth's umbra and penumbra during lunar eclipses.

- The Slip Explorer turns a scheduling question ("what if we launch late?") into one chart.

- A small astronaut guide walks new visitors through the app.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy and honesty: every number traces to NASA or JPL data and is checked against independent references; the app states its limits (for example, sites outside the polar terrain data use a flat horizon, and the polar points are labelled as reference points, not official landing coordinates).

- Two audiences: Simple mode gives a plain answer; Expert mode adds instrument readouts, definitions and CSV.

- Accessibility: colour palettes tested for colour blindness and contrast, full keyboard use, reduced-motion support and phone layouts.

- Speed: heavy calculations run in the background so controls respond instantly.

- Privacy and access: no accounts and no tracking; favourites and recent sites stay in your own browser; free to use from any device.
